title: 18 days ago I started an underwater PvP game with AI agents. Today the playtest is open
author: BHave_TRO
selftext:
I'm a single developer. On 15 October I made the first commit of STOREGGA, an online submarine combat game in Unreal Engine 5: humans fly subs, the Vael, a hidden people of the deep, ride sharks and grown living war-vessels. Since then AI agents have written nearly all of it, and I wanted to see if a game made this way can look and play like a game, not a demo.

**Where the AI is, part by part**

* **Code** (C++ game, Go match server, Python tools): Claude Code agents. I write the design decisions and review every merge; 365 automated tests and bot matches between two PCs gate each one.
* **3D models:** mostly agents writing Blender Python scripts, so every model can be rebuilt from a committed script. The new shark, its rider and the Hunter come from Meshy and were then cleaned up and baked by agents in Blender.
* **Sound:** no audio model. Agents wrote small DSP recipes in Python (sonar pings, torpedo whine, hull stress), mixed with free recordings from the Sonniss GDC bundle.
* **Concept art:** Google image generation, labelled. **Trailer music:** Google Flow Music.
* **Textures of the arenas:** my own photos, made tileable.
* **While you play, nothing is generated.** The bots are plain autopilots.

**What was hard**

* Code comes fast. Looks don't. Water, bubbles and light have taken many rounds and still aren't where I want them.
* Agents report success happily. Things only got reliable when "done" meant a command printed the expected result.
* This week the first run against live data showed that my own playtest metrics script would have thrown away every real match: the game calls its team mode "deathmatch" internally, the script looked for "Line War". The tests had passed, because they used the same wrong name.

**Numbers:** 18 days, 8 playtest builds, 1,618 commits, 73 written design decisions, 1 human.
